US indicts three men over alleged 'terror' attacks in US and Europe, including UK air base plotBy Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and APPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
Prosecutors in the United States have charged three men they describe as Iranian-backed operatives over their alleged role in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across the US and Europe, including a plot targeting the United Kingdom’s Fairford air base.
The Department of Justice said on Tuesday that the three men acted in support of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Iraq’s Kataib Hezbollah.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Is Iran planning attacks on Americans; why is the US on alert?list 2 of 3UK prosecutors charge two after RAF Fairford incidentlist 3 of 3US moves aircraft from second UK base over ‘threat from Iran’end of list
It identified the men as Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, who face what it called “terrorism-related offenses”.
Al-Saadi is already in jail in New York. Prosecutors did not disclose the whereabouts of Mohajeri and al-Hassani.
The charges announced on Tuesday centre on RAF Fairford in southwest England, where US forces and bombers had been stationed. The US had used the base to deploy bombers in its war against Iran.
Police were called to the Fairford site in September after a local farmer reported seeing a group of men with several white vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.

Tigrayan children gather in a classroom at an elementary school being used as a shelter for internally displaced people in Abi Adi, Tigray, northern Ethiopia, on May 11, 2021 [Ben Curtis/AP]By Million GebrekidanPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
Abi Adi, Tigray, Ethiopia – Classrooms that once echoed with the voices of students have become homes for families displaced by the war in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region.
At a former high school in Abi Adi, families who fled Western Tigray have spent years waiting to return home. Mattresses, cooking utensils and personal belongings have replaced school furniture as families share rooms originally designed for students.
What was supposed to be temporary shelter is now where children are growing up far from home.
“We thought we would stay here for a few months before returning home. It has been years now. Our children are growing up in this school, and we still don’t know when we will be able to go back,” said Tewolde, who was displaced from Setit Humera in Western Tigray.
His hopes of returning have been further undermined by renewed fighting, four years after Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed an agreement to end their devastating war.
The Pretoria agreement, signed in November 2022, ended two years of war that left an estimated 500,000 people dead, including from violence, famine and the collapse of healthcare, and displaced millions. But it left major political and territorial disputes unresolved, particularly over Western Tigray, where Amhara forces took control during the war.
The area remains disputed, and the return of displaced Tigrayans has been one of the most contentious outstanding issues.

Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has condemned the United Nations climate talks as hypocritical and urged world leaders to put people and planet ahead of profits and power.
Thunberg made the comments on Tuesday as she arrived at the COP31 conference in the Turkish resort city of Antalya.

The talks follow a year of deadly climate-related disasters, including heatwaves and floods, and another energy shock caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.

A view of Phase 12 of the South Pars gas field facilities near the southern Iranian town of Kangan, on the shore of the Gulf [File: AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 10 Nov 202610 Nov 2026
Iranian authorities have contained a fire that broke out on a platform in South Pars gas field, the world’s largest offshore natural gas field.
The Pars Oil and Gas Company said the fire broke out on Tuesday on a gas platform in Phase 14 of the South Pars field and was extinguished immediately, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported.

“During the incident, 17 workers jumped into the sea to save their lives; rescue operations for them are currently underway,” Kourosh Dehghan, Bushehr Province’s director general of crisis management, told Fars.
“Further details regarding the scale of the incident and the condition of the workers will be announced later,” Dehghan added.
Bushehr’s crisis management office later said all 17 workers were in good condition after boarding lifeboats and rescue craft, and that three heavy rescue vessels had been sent to the platform to bring them back.
Officials are considering a gas leak or an operational mishap as possible causes for the fire, Fars said.
The news agency added that the platform accounts for only 14.5 million cubic metres of South Pars’s total daily production of more than 700 million cubic metres of gas.
Iran shares the reservoir with major gas exporter Qatar, which calls its portion the North Dome.

The Kremlin is seen through Christmas decorations on the bank of the Moskva River in central Moscow, Russia [File: Alexander Nemenov/AFP]By AFP and News AgenciesPublished On 10 Nov 202610 Nov 2026
Russia has expelled a Moldovan diplomat in retaliation for Chisinau’s expulsion of a Russian embassy employee over the crash of a drone in Moldova.
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Tuesday that it had summoned Moldova’s ambassador, Lilian Darii, and informed him that a member of the Moldovan embassy’s staff had been declared unacceptable “on the basis of the principle of reciprocity”.

“A strong protest was lodged with the ambassador after the Moldovan authorities on October 23 declared an employee of the Russian embassy in Chisinau persona non grata,” the ministry said in a statement.
It said Moldova’s decision was made “under the formal pretext of the alleged discovery on the territory of the republic of debris of an unmanned aerial vehicle carrying explosives”, calling it “another unfriendly step”.
The ministry said the “true goal” of the move was “to further undermine the centuries-long history of Russian-Moldovan relations”.
‘Crashed near homes’
Last month, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said a “Russian attack drone” had violated the country’s airspace and “crashed near homes and an energy facility”.
Moldova then declared a staff member of the Russian embassy “persona non grata”.
